blocks.text: Redis is a server that holds data in RAM and answers by key. You give it a name, it gives you the value. Because nothing is read from disk on the request path, a lookup usually takes well under a millisecond.

Think of it as a shared dictionary that every instance of your app can reach over the network. The values are not only strings. Redis also has lists, sets, hashes and sorted sets built in, and each one has commands that run on the server.
Commands run one at a time on a single thread. That is why `INCR` is safe when a hundred clients call it at once: no two commands ever interleave.
Start a server and connect

blocks.code:
docker run -d --name redis -p 6379:6379 redis:8
docker exec -it redis redis-cli
127.0.0.1:6379> PING
PONG

SET user:42:name "Asha"        # OK
GET user:42:name               # "Asha"
EXISTS user:42:name            # (integer) 1
DEL user:42:name               # (integer) 1
GET user:42:name               # (nil)

SET otp:42 "918273" EX 300     # expires after 300 seconds
TTL otp:42                     # (integer) 300, counts down
TTL user:42:name               # -2 = key does not exist, -1 = no expiry

INCR page:home:views           # (integer) 1, atomic counter
INCRBY page:home:views 10      # (integer) 11

items: Name keys with colons, from general to specific: `user:42:cart`. Redis does not care, but people and tools do.
Give cache keys an expiry. A cache with no TTL grows until memory runs out.

blocks.text: **Trap.** `KEYS *` walks every key and blocks the server while it does. It is fine on your laptop and an outage in production. Use `SCAN 0 MATCH user:* COUNT 100`, which returns a page and a cursor.
Try it here

A small Redis look-alike written in this page. It understands about 25 commands (strings, expiry, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets). It is not a real server, so use it to build intuition and check anything important against real Redis.

modules.title: Data structures in a real app

lessons.title: Pick the structure that matches the question

rows: One object, updated field by field
Tags, "has this user seen it", common friends
Events that workers must not lose

blocks.code:
HSET user:42 name "Asha" city "Bengaluru"   # (integer) 2
HGET user:42 city                            # "Bengaluru"

RPUSH jobs "resize:1" "resize:2"             # (integer) 2
LPOP jobs                                    # "resize:1"

SADD post:9:tags redis cache redis           # (integer) 2, duplicate ignored

ZADD board 120 asha 95 ravi 140 meera        # (integer) 3
ZRANGE board 0 2 REV WITHSCORES              # meera 140, asha 120, ravi 95

blocks.text: The most common pattern. Ask Redis first. On a miss, read the database, store the answer with a TTL, return it. On a write, update the database and delete the key.
**Trap.** Treat Redis as optional in this pattern. If it is down, the code should fall through to the database, not return an error.

items: **Pipeline.** Send many commands in one network round trip. It saves time and gives no atomicity.
**MULTI / EXEC.** Queue commands and run them as one uninterrupted block. There is no rollback: if one command fails, the others still apply.
**WATCH.** Optimistic lock. `EXEC` returns nil if a watched key changed, and you retry.
**Lua script.** Runs on the server as one atomic step. Use it for "read, decide, write".

blocks.code:
MULTI
DECRBY stock:sku9 1
RPUSH orders "sku9:user42"
EXEC                           # 1) (integer) 4   2) (integer) 1

blocks.text: When a popular key expires, every request misses at once and they all hit the database together. Three fixes, usually combined:

items: Add random jitter to TTLs (300 seconds plus 0 to 60) so keys do not expire together.
Let one request rebuild the value behind a short lock while the others wait or serve the old value.
Refresh hot keys in the background before they expire.

blocks.text: Also cache "not found" for a short time. Otherwise a request for an id that does not exist reaches the database every time.
Memory limit and eviction

blocks.code:
maxmemory 2gb
maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru

items: `noeviction` (default): writes fail when memory is full. Right when Redis is your source of truth.
`allkeys-lru` / `allkeys-lfu`: drop the least recently or least frequently used key. Right for a pure cache.
`volatile-ttl`, `volatile-lru`: only evict keys that have an expiry.

blocks.text: Fixed window: count requests per user per minute. The script keeps the increment and the expiry in one atomic step, so a crash between them cannot leave a counter that never expires.

blocks.code:
-- KEYS[1] = rate:user42:202611131045   ARGV[1] = window seconds
local n = redis.call('INCR', KEYS[1])
if n == 1 then redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[1]) end
return n                       -- caller rejects when n > limit

blocks.text: A fixed window allows a burst of twice the limit across the boundary. For a smoother limit, keep request timestamps in a sorted set, remove the ones older than the window with `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE`, and count the rest with `ZCARD`.

items: **Pub/Sub** delivers to whoever is connected right now. A subscriber that is offline misses the message. Good for live notifications, wrong for work that must happen.
**Streams** store the messages. A consumer group gives each message to one worker, and the worker confirms with `XACK`. Unconfirmed messages can be claimed by another worker.

blocks.code:
XADD orders * user 42 sku 9                       # "1731490000000-0"
XGROUP CREATE orders billing $ MKSTREAM
XREADGROUP GROUP billing w1 COUNT 10 BLOCK 5000 STREAMS orders >
XACK orders billing 1731490000000-0

blocks.text: A lock is one command: `SET lock:report 7f3a NX PX 30000`. The random value is your token. Release only if the token is still yours, in a script, so you never delete a lock someone else took after yours expired.
**Trap.** A Redis lock can expire while its holder is paused. It prevents duplicate work most of the time. Where a double run would corrupt data, also check a version number in the database.
Persistence

rows: Full copy of memory written to disk on a schedule
Every write appended to a log; `appendfsync everysec`
AOF for safety, RDB for backups

items: **Replication.** Replicas copy the primary asynchronously. A write acknowledged by the primary can be lost if it dies before the replica receives it.
**Sentinel.** Separate processes that watch the primary and promote a replica when it fails. One dataset, automatic failover.
**Cluster.** Splits keys across primaries using 16,384 hash slots. The slot is CRC16 of the key, modulo 16384. Use it when the data or the write load no longer fits one machine.

blocks.text: In Cluster, a multi-key command only works when all keys are in the same slot. Force that with a hash tag: only the part in braces is hashed, so `{user:42}:cart` and `{user:42}:profile` land together.
Operating it

items: Find slow commands with `SLOWLOG GET 10`, memory with `INFO memory` and `MEMORY USAGE key`.
A big key (a list with millions of items) makes one command slow, and one slow command delays everyone. Delete big keys with `UNLINK`, which frees memory in the background.
Watch the hit rate: `keyspace_hits / (keyspace_hits + keyspace_misses)` from `INFO stats`.
Never expose port 6379 to the internet. Set a password or ACL users, bind to private addresses, use TLS between networks.
Redis 8 folded JSON, search, time series and probabilistic types into the main server. Valkey is the open-source fork many cloud providers now run; the commands in this guide work on both.

blocks.text: Practice projects

items: Level 1: an OTP store. Six digits, 5 minute expiry, at most 3 attempts using `INCR`.
Level 2: put cache-aside in front of one slow endpoint and measure latency before and after.
Level 3: a leaderboard API with a sorted set, a rate limiter in Lua, and a worker reading a Stream with a consumer group.

blocks.title: Why is Redis fast?
blocks.text: Data lives in memory, the structures are simple and purpose-built, and commands run on one thread so there is no locking. Network I/O is multiplexed, so one thread serves thousands of connections.

blocks.title: What happens when memory is full?
blocks.text: It depends on `maxmemory-policy`. With `noeviction` writes return an error. With an LRU or LFU policy Redis removes keys to make room.

blocks.title: MULTI/EXEC or Lua?
blocks.text: MULTI runs a fixed list of commands together. Lua can read a value and decide what to write based on it, all in one atomic step. Use Lua when the logic branches.

blocks.title: Pub/Sub or Streams?
blocks.text: Pub/Sub does not store anything, so offline subscribers miss messages. Streams store entries, support consumer groups and acknowledgements, and can be replayed.

blocks.title: How do you keep cache and database consistent?
blocks.text: Write the database first, then delete the cache key, and keep a TTL as a safety net. Accept a short stale window, or use change data capture to invalidate when you cannot.

blocks.title: Why can Redis lose an acknowledged write?
blocks.text: Replication is asynchronous and AOF usually syncs once a second. A crash in that gap loses the latest writes. `WAIT` reduces the risk and does not remove it.

blocks.title: What is a hash tag?
blocks.text: The part of a key inside braces. In Cluster only that part decides the slot, which lets related keys share a slot so multi-key commands and scripts work.

Kafka is a set of servers that store events in the order they arrived. An event is a small record such as "order 17 was placed". Producers add events to the end. Consumers read forward from wherever they stopped.

The difference from a normal queue is that reading does not remove anything. Events stay for a set time, seven days by default, so several teams can read the same events independently and a new service can replay history.
Use it when many systems need to react to the same facts, or when traffic arrives faster than the receiver can process it and you need a buffer that does not lose data.
The seven words

rows: One Kafka server. A cluster is several brokers.
A named stream of events, like `orders`.
A topic is split into partitions. Each one is its own ordered log, stored on a broker.
The position of an event inside a partition: 0, 1, 2 and so on.
Consumers sharing one name. Kafka gives each partition to exactly one of them, so the group shares the work.

lessons.title: Start a broker and use the CLI

blocks.code:
docker run -d --name kafka -p 9092:9092 apache/kafka:latest
docker exec -it kafka bash
cd /opt/kafka/bin

# create a topic with 3 partitions
./kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --create \
  --topic orders --partitions 3 --replication-factor 1

# produce: type key:value, one per line
./kafka-console-producer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic orders \
  --reader-property parse.key=true --reader-property key.separator=:
> order-1:placed
> order-2:placed
> order-1:paid
> order-3:placed

# consume in a second terminal, as group "billing"
./kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic orders \
  --group billing --from-beginning \
  --formatter-property print.key=true --formatter-property print.partition=true \
  --formatter-property print.offset=true
Partition:0  Offset:0  order-2  placed
Partition:0  Offset:1  order-3  placed
Partition:1  Offset:0  order-1  placed
Partition:1  Offset:1  order-1  paid

# where is the group, and how far behind?
./kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --describe --group billing
GROUP    TOPIC   PARTITION  CURRENT-OFFSET  LOG-END-OFFSET  LAG
billing  orders  0          2               2               0
billing  orders  1          2               2               0
billing  orders  2          0               0               0

blocks.text: Both `order-1` events are in partition 1, in the order they were sent. The output above is from a real run on Kafka 4.3.1. On Kafka 3.x write `--property` in place of `--reader-property` and `--formatter-property`; version 4 still accepts the old name with a deprecation warning.
The last command prints, per partition, `CURRENT-OFFSET`, `LOG-END-OFFSET` and `LAG`. Lag is how many events are waiting. It is the first number to check when something looks slow.

A simplified model of one topic, `orders`, with 3 partitions and one consumer group. The same key always lands in the same partition. Real Kafka picks the partition with a murmur2 hash and assigns partitions with a configurable strategy; the idea is the same.

Things to notice. Order is kept inside a partition, not across the topic. Removing a consumer moves its partitions to the others. A fourth consumer gets nothing, because there are only three partitions.

Kafka guarantees order only within one partition. Events with the same key go to the same partition, so choose the key by asking "which events must stay in order?". For orders that is the order id. For a wallet it is the user id.
**Trap.** Adding partitions later changes which partition a key maps to, and old and new events for the same key may be read out of order. Pick the partition count with room to grow.

A consumer saves its position by committing an offset. When it restarts, or its partition moves to another consumer, reading resumes from the last commit. When you commit decides what happens on a crash.

rows: Transactions, or at least once plus an idempotent handler

blocks.text: Most systems run at least once and make the handler safe to repeat: keep the event id in the database with a unique constraint, or use an upsert.

blocks.code:
# Python, package "confluent-kafka"
import json
from confluent_kafka import Producer, Consumer

p = Producer({"bootstrap.servers": "localhost:9092", "enable.idempotence": True})
p.produce("orders", key="order-17", value=json.dumps({"total": 499}))
p.flush()

c = Consumer({
    "bootstrap.servers": "localhost:9092",
    "group.id": "billing",
    "auto.offset.reset": "earliest",
    "enable.auto.commit": False,
})
c.subscribe(["orders"])
while True:
    msg = c.poll(1.0)
    if msg is None or msg.error():
        continue
    charge(json.loads(msg.value()))
    c.commit(message=msg)          # process first, then commit = at least once

blocks.text: For new Node projects also look at Confluent's own client, `@confluentinc/kafka-javascript`. It offers an API close to kafkajs and is the one that gets active releases. On a broker that has just started, kafkajs may log "coordinator is loading" once or twice and then continue; it retries by itself.
Producer settings that matter

items: `acks=all`: the write is confirmed only after the in-sync replicas have it. `acks=1` is faster and can lose data when a leader dies.
`enable.idempotence=true`: retries cannot create duplicates or reorder events. It is the default in current clients.
`linger.ms` and `batch.size`: wait a few milliseconds to send events in batches. Much higher throughput for a small delay.
`compression.type=lz4` or `zstd`: smaller batches on the wire and on disk.

blocks.text: Each partition has one leader and several followers on other brokers. Producers and consumers talk to the leader. Followers that are caught up form the in-sync replica set (ISR). If the leader dies, a member of the ISR takes over.

The standard safe setup is replication factor 3, `min.insync.replicas=2` and `acks=all`. You can lose one broker with no data loss and no downtime. With two brokers gone, writes are refused instead of being accepted unsafely.
Retention and compaction

items: **Delete** (default): events older than `retention.ms`, or beyond `retention.bytes`, are removed. Right for event history.
**Compact**: Kafka keeps at least the latest event for every key and removes older ones. Right for "current state" topics such as user settings. An event with a null value deletes the key.

lessons.title: Failures: retry topics and a dead letter topic

blocks.text: One bad event must not block a partition forever. After a few attempts, publish it to a retry topic that is consumed with a delay, and after the last attempt to a dead letter topic, for example `orders.dlq`, with the error in a header. Then commit and move on. Alert on the dead letter topic and build a way to replay it.
**Trap.** Moving an event to a retry topic breaks ordering for its key. If order matters, park all later events for that key too, or stop the partition and page someone.

Kafka transactions let a consumer read from one topic, write to another and commit its offset as a single atomic step. Consumers with `isolation.level=read_committed` never see the aborted writes. This covers Kafka-to-Kafka pipelines only.

The moment a database is involved, use the outbox pattern. In the same database transaction that changes the order, insert a row into an `outbox` table. A separate process, often Debezium reading the database log, publishes those rows to Kafka. The database change and the event can no longer disagree.
Schemas

Producers and consumers are deployed at different times, so the event format is a contract. A schema registry stores Avro, Protobuf or JSON Schema definitions and rejects a change that would break readers. The everyday rule for backward compatibility: you may add a field with a default and you may not remove or rename a field that readers use.
Connect and stream processing

items: **Kafka Connect** moves data in and out without custom code. Source connectors read from systems such as Postgres (change data capture); sink connectors write to systems such as Elasticsearch or S3.
**Kafka Streams** is a Java library for transforming streams: filter, join, count per time window. It keeps state locally and backs it up to Kafka.
**Flink** and **ksqlDB** do the same job as separate systems, Flink with more power and ksqlDB with SQL.

blocks.text: When a consumer joins, leaves or stops polling, the group reassigns partitions. That is a rebalance, and frequent ones stall processing. The usual causes and fixes:

items: A handler slower than `max.poll.interval.ms` (5 minutes by default) gets the consumer removed. Lower `max.poll.records` or move slow work off the polling loop.

Rolling deploys shuffle everything. Use the cooperative sticky assignor, or the newer consumer group protocol in Kafka 4, so only the affected partitions move. Static membership (`group.instance.id`) lets a restarted pod keep its partitions.
Lag that grows steadily means consumers are too slow. Add consumers up to the partition count, speed up the handler, or add partitions.

blocks.text: Sizing, cluster and security

items: Partition count sets the maximum number of consumers working in parallel. Start from target throughput divided by what one consumer handles, then add headroom. Thousands of tiny partitions cost memory and slow recovery.
Since Kafka 4.0 there is no ZooKeeper. A group of controller nodes runs the metadata using KRaft, Kafka's own Raft implementation.
Turn on TLS for traffic, SASL for identity and ACLs so each service can touch only its own topics and groups.
Watch under-replicated partitions, consumer lag, request latency and disk usage. Mirror topics to another region with MirrorMaker 2 when you need disaster recovery.

rows: What fits in RAM; trim with `MAXLEN`
One key lives on one node
A cluster to operate, or a managed service
Background jobs and modest event flow inside one product
A company-wide event backbone, analytics pipelines, replay

blocks.text: Do not reach for Kafka for request and reply between two services, for a small task queue, or when a few hundred events a minute would be served by a database table.
Practice projects

items: Level 1: produce 20 keyed events from the CLI and explain the partition and offset of each line the consumer prints.
Level 2: an order service that publishes and a billing consumer with manual commits. Kill the consumer mid-batch and prove nothing is charged twice.
Level 3: add a retry topic and a dead letter topic, an outbox table, and a dashboard panel for consumer lag.

blocks.title: How is Kafka different from a queue like RabbitMQ?
blocks.text: A queue hands each message to one worker and deletes it. Kafka keeps an ordered log; each consumer group tracks its own position, so many groups read the same events and can replay them.

blocks.title: Where is ordering guaranteed?
blocks.text: Within a single partition only. Use the same key for events that must stay in order.

blocks.title: Two consumers in one group, one partition. What happens?
blocks.text: One consumer gets the partition and the other sits idle as a standby. Parallelism is capped by the partition count.

blocks.title: What does acks=all with min.insync.replicas=2 give you?
blocks.text: A write succeeds only when at least two replicas have it, so losing one broker loses no acknowledged data. If fewer than two replicas are in sync, the producer gets an error.

blocks.title: Why can a consumer see the same event twice?
blocks.text: It processed the event and crashed, or lost its partition in a rebalance, before committing the offset. The next owner starts from the last commit.

blocks.title: What is consumer lag?
blocks.text: The log end offset minus the group's committed offset, per partition. It is the number of events waiting to be processed.

blocks.title: When do you use a compacted topic?
blocks.text: When consumers need the latest value per key, not the full history: configuration, profiles, a changelog used to rebuild state.

blocks.title: What problem does the outbox pattern solve?
blocks.text: Writing to a database and publishing to Kafka are two systems, and one can fail after the other succeeded. Writing the event to an outbox table in the same transaction makes them succeed or fail together.

RabbitMQ is a message broker. Think of a post office. One program hands it a message. RabbitMQ keeps the message in a queue, delivers it to a program that is ready for it, and deletes it once that program says the work is done.
The sender does not wait and does not need to know who will do the work. That is the point. A web request can say "send this email" and return at once, while a worker sends the email a moment later.
Use it for background jobs, for spreading work across several workers, and for letting one service tell others that something happened without calling each of them.
The six words

rows: The sorting desk. Producers send to an exchange, never straight to a queue.
A line of messages waiting for a consumer.
A rule that connects an exchange to a queue.
A label on each message that the exchange compares with the bindings.
A program that receives messages and acknowledges them.

blocks.code:
docker run -d --name rabbit --hostname rabbit --user rabbitmq \
  -p 5672:5672 -p 15672:15672 rabbitmq:4-management

docker exec rabbit rabbitmq-diagnostics -q ping
Ping succeeded

blocks.text: Port 5672 is for your programs. Port 15672 is the management screen at `http://localhost:15672`, where the built-in user is `guest` with password `guest`. That user works only from the same machine.

**Trap.** On this Mac the 4.4.0 image exited at once without `--user rabbitmq`, with "Error when reading /var/lib/rabbitmq/.erlang.cookie: eacces" in `docker logs rabbit`. Running the container as the `rabbitmq` user fixed it. `--hostname` matters too: RabbitMQ stores data under its host name, so keep it stable.

docker exec -it rabbit bash

rabbitmqadmin declare queue --name tasks --durable true
rabbitmqadmin publish message -k tasks -m "resize photo 1"
Message published and routed successfully
rabbitmqadmin publish message -k tasks -m "resize photo 2"

rabbitmqctl list_queues name messages
tasks   2

rabbitmqadmin get messages -q tasks       # takes one message off the queue

rabbitmqadmin publish message -k nowhere -m "lost?"
Message published but NOT routed

items: These first messages name no exchange, so they go to the default exchange. It delivers to the queue whose name equals the routing key.
The last line is the first lesson in reliability. A message that matches no queue is dropped. RabbitMQ does not keep it for later.
The image ships `rabbitmqadmin` version 2. Older guides show version 1 syntax such as `rabbitmqadmin declare queue name=tasks`, which no longer works.

rows: Queues whose binding key equals the routing key exactly
Sending each kind of job to its own queue
Every bound queue, ignoring the routing key
Telling everyone: cache clear, config changed
Queues whose binding pattern matches. `*` is exactly one word, `#` is zero or more words
Events with structured names such as `order.paid`
Queues whose binding matches message headers

rabbitmqadmin declare exchange --name orders --type topic --durable true
rabbitmqadmin declare queue --name billing --durable true

  --destination billing --routing-key order.paid

rabbitmqctl list_queues name messages
billing 1       # order.paid only
emails  2       # order.paid and order.placed
audit   3       # everything

blocks.text: One message became three copies, one per matching queue. Each queue is then read independently. This is how one event feeds several services.
Try the routing
A model of the three bindings above. Change the exchange type and the routing key, then send. It follows the documented matching rules and is not a real broker.
Four settings work together. Leave one out and a restart or a crash can lose work.

items: **Durable queue.** The queue itself survives a broker restart.
**Persistent message.** The message is written to disk, not held only in memory.
**Publisher confirm.** The producer waits until the broker says "stored".
**Manual acknowledgement.** The consumer says "done" only after the work has finished. If it crashes first, the broker gives the message to another consumer.

blocks.text: **Prefetch** limits how many unacknowledged messages one consumer may hold. With no limit, the broker pushes everything to the first worker that connects and the others sit idle.
A real run where `resize` fails on photo 2:

**Trap.** Declaring a queue that already exists with different settings fails: "PRECONDITION_FAILED - inequivalent arg 'x-dead-letter-exchange' for queue 'jobs'". Keep the declaration in one shared place, as `setup` does here. To change a queue's settings you delete it and create it again.
Code: Python

blocks.code:
# package "pika" 1.5 or newer
import json, threading, pika

conn = pika.Connection(pika.ConnectionParameters("localhost"))
ch = conn.channel()
ch.queue_declare(queue="emails_out", durable=True)

ch.basic_publish(
    exchange="",
    routing_key="emails_out",
    body=json.dumps({"to": "asha@example.com"}),
    properties=pika.BasicProperties(delivery_mode=2),   # 2 = persistent
)

done = threading.Event()

def handle(ch, method, properties, body):
    send(json.loads(body))
    ch.basic_ack(delivery_tag=method.delivery_tag)
    done.set()

ch.basic_qos(prefetch_count=1)
ch.basic_consume(queue="emails_out", on_message_callback=handle)
done.wait(timeout=15)                # a real worker waits forever
conn.close()

blocks.text: Most older examples use `pika.BlockingConnection` with `ch.start_consuming()`. It still runs on pika 1.5 and prints a warning that it will be removed in pika 2.0.

With manual acknowledgements you get at-least-once delivery. A worker can finish the job and crash before it acknowledges, and the message is delivered again. Make handlers safe to repeat: record the message id in your database with a unique constraint, or write the result as an upsert.

Order is kept for one queue with one consumer. Several consumers, or a message put back on the queue, break that order. If order matters for a customer, send all of that customer's messages to the same queue and read it with one consumer.

A message is **dead-lettered** when a consumer rejects it without requeue, when it sits longer than its time-to-live, or when the queue is full. If the queue names a dead letter exchange, the message is sent there instead of being deleted. You saw that with photo 2.

For a delayed retry, dead-letter into a wait queue that has no consumers and a time-to-live of, say, 30 seconds, and make that queue dead-letter back to the work queue. The message returns by itself after the delay. Count the attempts from the `x-death` header and park the message in a failed queue after a few tries.

**Trap.** `nack` with requeue set to true puts the message straight back at the front. A message that always fails then loops at full speed. In a test for this guide, a quorum queue on RabbitMQ 4.4 delivered one always-requeued message 4,432 times in four seconds and never gave up. Reject without requeue and let a dead letter exchange handle the retry.
Queue types

rows: One node. If that node is down, the queue is unavailable
Data you can afford to lose or rebuild; temporary queues
Copied to several nodes, agreed by majority
An append-only log on disk; reading does not remove messages
Replay and many independent readers, in the style of Kafka

blocks.text: RabbitMQ 4 removed the old mirrored classic queues. Replication now means quorum queues or streams.

rabbitmqadmin publish message -k payments -m "pay order 17"
rabbitmq-queues quorum_status payments  # rabbit1 leader, rabbit2 and rabbit3 followers

docker compose stop rabbit1             # stop the node that leads the queue
rabbitmqctl list_queues name type leader messages
payments  quorum  rabbit@rabbit3  1     # new leader, message still there

blocks.text: Nodes trust each other only when they share the same Erlang cookie, so treat it as a secret in real deployments. The environment variable used here is a shortcut for a laptop; the broker logs a warning when it is set. As with ZooKeeper, use an odd number of nodes: a quorum queue needs a majority of its copies to accept a write.
RabbitMQ is fastest when queues are short. A queue that only grows means consumers are too slow or absent. Two alarms protect the broker:

blocks.code:
rabbitmq-diagnostics status
Memory high watermark setting: 0.6 of available memory
Low free disk space watermark: 0.05 gb

rabbitmq-diagnostics check_local_alarms
Node rabbit@rabbit reported no local alarms

blocks.text: When memory passes the watermark or free disk falls below the limit, the broker stops accepting messages from producers until it recovers. Publishing appears to hang. Give queues a maximum length or a time-to-live so that a stuck consumer cannot fill the disk.

blocks.code:
rabbitmqctl add_vhost shop
rabbitmqctl add_user shopapp 'a-long-random-password'
rabbitmqctl set_permissions -p shop shopapp "^shop\..*" "^shop\..*" "^shop\..*"

rabbitmqctl list_permissions -p shop
user     configure   write       read
shopapp  ^shop\..*   ^shop\..*   ^shop\..*

items: A virtual host is a separate space with its own exchanges and queues. Give each application or environment its own.
The three patterns say which names the user may create, publish to and read from.
Create your own users and remove `guest`. Use TLS on port 5671 between networks. Keep the management port off the public internet.

blocks.text: Connections and monitoring

items: Open one connection per process and keep it open. Use a channel per thread or per task. Opening a connection for every message is the most common cause of a slow, overloaded broker.
Reconnect with a delay when the connection drops, and declare queues again on reconnect.
Watch per queue: messages ready, messages unacknowledged, consumer count, publish and acknowledge rates. Ready growing means too few consumers. Unacknowledged growing means stuck consumers.
The broker serves metrics for Prometheus on port 15692. `rabbitmq-diagnostics check_running` exits with 0 when the node is healthy, which suits a container health check.

rows: A queue: deliver each message to a worker, then delete it
A log: keep every event, readers track their own position
Simple: a topic and a key that picks the partition
Gone, unless you use a stream
Still there until retention removes it; can be replayed
Acknowledge, reject, retry, delay, priority, time-to-live
Commit an offset; retries need extra topics
Tens of thousands of messages a second on a node
Hundreds of thousands and more, with batching
Background jobs, task distribution, request and reply, complex routing
Event history, analytics pipelines, many teams reading the same stream

blocks.text: Many systems use both: RabbitMQ for "do this job", Kafka for "this happened". Throughput figures are typical ranges, not something measured for this guide.
Practice projects

items: Level 1: publish five messages from the terminal, read two, and explain every number `list_queues` prints.
Level 2: run the producer and two workers. Kill one worker mid-job and watch the other receive its message.
Level 3: add a 30 second retry queue in front of the failed queue, then build the three-node cluster and stop the leader of a quorum queue.

blocks.title: Exchange or queue: where does a producer send?
blocks.text: Always to an exchange. The exchange uses bindings and the routing key to decide which queues get a copy. Sending "to a queue" uses the default exchange behind the scenes.

blocks.title: What is the difference between * and # in a topic binding?
blocks.text: `*` matches exactly one word. `#` matches zero or more words. `order.*` matches `order.paid` and not `order.paid.eu`; `order.#` matches both.

blocks.title: What happens to a message that matches no queue?
blocks.text: It is dropped. To catch these, set an alternate exchange or publish with the mandatory flag so the broker returns it.

blocks.title: Why set prefetch?
blocks.text: It caps unacknowledged messages per consumer, so work is shared fairly and a slow worker does not hoard messages in memory.

blocks.title: What do you need so a broker restart loses nothing?
blocks.text: A durable queue, persistent messages, publisher confirms, and manual acknowledgements after the work is done. For a node failure, also a quorum queue.

blocks.title: What is a dead letter exchange?
blocks.text: An exchange that receives messages a queue gives up on: rejected without requeue, expired, or pushed out by a length limit. It is how failed messages are kept and retried.

blocks.title: Classic or quorum queue?
blocks.text: Quorum for data that matters, because it is copied to several nodes and survives a node failure. Classic for temporary or rebuildable data on one node.

blocks.title: When would you choose Kafka over RabbitMQ?
blocks.text: When events must be kept and replayed, when many independent readers need the same stream, or when the volume is very high.

Docker packs a program together with everything it needs to run, then runs that package the same way on any machine. You did not install Redis or Kafka for this guide. You ran a package someone else built.

Two words carry most of it. An **image** is the package: files plus the command to start. It never changes. A **container** is one running copy of an image, with its own files, its own network address and its own process list.

A container is not a virtual machine. It is a normal process that the operating system keeps separated from the others, so it starts in about a second. On a Mac, Docker Desktop runs one small Linux machine in the background and all containers live inside it.
The life of one container

blocks.code:
docker run -d --name redis -p 6379:6379 redis:8   # download the image if needed, start a container
docker ps                                          # what is running
NAMES   IMAGE     STATUS         PORTS
redis   redis:8   Up 2 seconds   0.0.0.0:6379->6379/tcp

docker logs redis                                  # what the program printed
docker exec redis redis-cli PING                   # run a command inside it
PONG
docker exec -it redis redis-cli                    # same, as an interactive shell

docker stop redis                                  # stop the process, keep the container
docker ps -a                                       # redis   Exited (0)
docker start redis                                 # run it again
docker rm -f redis                                 # stop and delete it

rows: Run in the background and give the terminal back.
A name you choose, used by every later command.
Port on your machine, then port in the container. Without it, nothing outside Docker can connect.
Set an environment variable for the program.
Keep the files at that path outside the container.
Join a network so containers find each other by name.
Delete the container when it exits. Good for one-off commands.
Image name and tag. The tag is the version.

blocks.text: **Trap.** "Container name already in use" means an old container with that name still exists, running or stopped. Remove it with `docker rm -f redis`. "Port is already allocated" means something else on your machine holds that port.
Try the flags
Tick the flags and read what changes. This is a model of the rules, not a running container.
Files written inside a container belong to that container. Delete it and start a new one, and Redis is empty. A volume is storage that Docker keeps separately and attaches at a path.

blocks.code:
docker volume create redis-data
docker run -d --name redis -v redis-data:/data redis:8 redis-server --appendonly yes
docker exec redis redis-cli SET city Bengaluru     # OK
docker rm -f redis                                 # container gone

docker run -d --name redis -v redis-data:/data redis:8 redis-server --appendonly yes
docker exec redis redis-cli GET city               # Bengaluru

blocks.text: A named volume (`redis-data:/data`) is managed by Docker and is right for database files. A bind mount (`./src:/app/src`) maps a folder from your machine and is right for source code you are editing.

blocks.code:
docker network create shop
docker run -d --name redis --network shop redis:8

docker run --rm --network shop redis:8 redis-cli -h redis PING
PONG
docker run --rm redis:8 redis-cli -h redis PING    # not on the network
Could not connect to Redis at redis:6379: Name or service not known

blocks.text: On a network you create, the container name works as a hostname. That is why app config says `redis://redis:6379` and not an IP address.
**Trap.** Inside a container, `localhost` is that container, not your Mac and not the Redis container. An app in a container that connects to `localhost:6379` finds nothing.

lessons.title: A Dockerfile for your own app

blocks.text: A Dockerfile is the recipe for an image. Each line adds a layer, and Docker reuses a layer when its inputs have not changed. Copying `package.json` before the rest of the code means dependencies are reinstalled only when they change.

blocks.code:
FROM node:22-alpine AS deps
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json ./
RUN npm install --omit=dev

FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=deps /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY . .
USER node
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

blocks.text: Add a `.dockerignore` file with `node_modules` and `.git` so they are not copied in. Build with `docker build -t shop-api ./app`.

lessons.title: Compose: the whole stack in one file

blocks.text: Compose starts several containers together, on one shared network, from a file you keep in the repository. This file runs Redis, Kafka and a small Node API that counts page views in Redis and publishes each view to Kafka.

blocks.code:
services:
  redis:
    image: redis:8
    command: redis-server --appendonly yes
    volumes:
      - redis-data:/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5

  kafka:
    image: apache/kafka:latest
    ports:
      - "9092:9092"
    environment:
      KAFKA_NODE_ID: 1
      KAFKA_PROCESS_ROLES: broker,controller
      KAFKA_CONTROLLER_QUORUM_VOTERS: 1@kafka:9093
      KAFKA_CONTROLLER_LISTENER_NAMES: CONTROLLER
      KAFKA_LISTENERS: INTERNAL://:19092,HOST://:9092,CONTROLLER://:9093
      KAFKA_ADVERTISED_LISTENERS: INTERNAL://kafka:19092,HOST://localhost:9092
      KAFKA_LISTENER_SECURITY_PROTOCOL_MAP: INTERNAL:PLAINTEXT,HOST:PLAINTEXT,CONTROLLER:PLAINTEXT
      KAFKA_INTER_BROKER_LISTENER_NAME: INTERNAL
      KAFKA_OFFSETS_TOPIC_REPLICATION_FACTOR: 1
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "/opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:19092 --list"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 10s
      retries: 10

  api:
    build: ./app
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    environment:
      REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379
      KAFKA_BROKER: kafka:19092
    depends_on:
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy
      kafka:
        condition: service_healthy

volumes:
  redis-data:

docker compose up -d --build       # build the api image, start everything
docker compose ps
SERVICE   STATUS                    PORTS
api       Up 4 seconds              0.0.0.0:3000->3000/tcp
kafka     Up 46 seconds (healthy)   0.0.0.0:9092->9092/tcp
redis     Up 46 seconds (healthy)   6379/tcp

curl localhost:3000                # views: 1
curl localhost:3000                # views: 2
docker compose logs -f api         # follow one service's output
docker compose down                # stop and remove containers, keep the volume
docker compose up -d
curl localhost:3000                # views: 3, the count survived
docker compose down -v             # also delete the volume

blocks.text: The API takes a few seconds to connect before it answers. Redis has no `ports` entry on purpose: only the API needs it, and the API reaches it over the Compose network.

A Kafka client connects twice. First to the address you gave it, to ask for the cluster layout. Then to the address the broker *advertises* for itself. If the broker advertises `localhost:9092`, a client in another container follows that to its own localhost and fails.

The fix is two listeners, as in the file above. `INTERNAL` advertises `kafka:19092` for other containers. `HOST` advertises `localhost:9092` for programs on your Mac. Each client uses the one that matches where it runs.

Plain `depends_on` waits only until the other container has started, not until the server inside is ready. Kafka takes several seconds to accept connections. A health check plus `condition: service_healthy` makes the API wait for a real answer. Your app should still retry its connections, because servers also restart later.
Limits and restarts

blocks.code:
docker run -d --name redis --memory 256m --cpus 1 --restart unless-stopped redis:8
docker stats --no-stream redis
redis   11.68MiB / 256MiB   0.37%

items: Without a memory limit, one container can take all the memory on the machine. With one, the container is killed when it goes over, so set Redis `maxmemory` below the limit.
`--restart unless-stopped` brings the container back after a crash or a reboot. `on-failure` restarts only on a non-zero exit.

blocks.text: Images: small, pinned, not root

items: Pin versions. `redis:8` and `apache/kafka:4.3.1` give the same result next month. `latest`, used in this guide for convenience, does not.
Use a small base (`-alpine` or `-slim`) and a multi-stage build so compilers and caches stay out of the final image. The API image above is 254 MB, most of it the Node runtime.
`USER node` in the Dockerfile runs the app as a normal user. If the app is broken into, the attacker is not root.
Never copy secrets into an image or write them in a Dockerfile. Anyone with the image can read them. Pass them at run time.

blocks.text: Stateful servers in containers

Redis and Kafka hold data, so they need more care than a stateless API. Give each one a volume, give Kafka brokers stable names, and stop them gracefully so they can flush to disk. In Kubernetes this is what a StatefulSet does. Many teams run their apps in containers and use a managed Redis and a managed Kafka instead.
Seeing and cleaning what Docker holds

blocks.code:
docker system df                   # space used by images, containers, volumes
docker image ls
docker volume ls
docker image prune                 # remove images nothing uses and nothing tags
docker system prune                # also stopped containers and unused networks

blocks.text: **Trap.** `docker system prune -a --volumes` deletes every unused image and every unused volume, including database files you may want. Read the confirmation line before you answer yes.
Practice projects

items: Level 1: start Redis, set a key, remove the container, start it again and explain why the key is gone.
Level 2: write the Compose file above from memory, then add a second API container and watch both share one counter.
Level 3: break the Kafka listeners on purpose (advertise only `localhost:9092`), read the error the API prints, and fix it.

blocks.title: Image or container?
blocks.text: An image is the read-only package. A container is a running copy of it with its own writable files. Many containers can run from one image.

blocks.title: How is a container different from a virtual machine?
blocks.text: A virtual machine runs a full operating system. A container is a process on the host's kernel, separated by the operating system, so it is smaller and starts in about a second.

blocks.title: What does -p 8080:80 mean?
blocks.text: Port 8080 on your machine forwards to port 80 inside the container. Host first, container second.

blocks.title: Where does data go when a container is removed?
blocks.text: Files in the container are lost. Files in a volume or a bind mount stay.

blocks.title: Why can the API reach Redis at the name redis?
blocks.text: Compose puts all services on one network, and Docker's built-in name lookup resolves each service name to its container.

blocks.title: Why does Kafka in Docker need two listeners?
blocks.text: Clients reconnect to the address the broker advertises. Containers need the service name, programs on the host need localhost, so the broker advertises one of each.

blocks.title: depends_on is set, yet the app fails at startup. Why?
blocks.text: Without a health condition, depends_on waits for the container to start, not for the server to be ready. Add a health check and `condition: service_healthy`, and retry in the app.

A cluster of servers has to agree on a few small facts. Which servers are alive? Which one is in charge? What is the current configuration? ZooKeeper is a small, very reliable store built to hold exactly those facts.

It looks like a file system. Data lives in a tree of nodes called **znodes**, each with a path such as `/brokers/ids/1` and a small value. Every server in a ZooKeeper group sees every change in the same order, so two clients can never both believe they are the leader.
It is not a database for your application data. A znode holds at most about 1 MB, and the whole tree sits in memory.
Start it and open the shell

blocks.code:
docker run -d --name zk -p 2181:2181 zookeeper:3.9
docker exec -it zk zkCli.sh
[zk: localhost:2181(CONNECTED) 0]

ls /                               # [zookeeper]
create /shop "hello"               # Created /shop
get /shop                          # hello
set /shop "v2"
get -s /shop                       # v2, then details: dataVersion = 1 ...
create /shop/config "retries=3"
ls /shop                           # [config]

create -e /shop/worker-1 "alive"   # -e: temporary, tied to this session
create -s /shop/job- "a"           # -s: ZooKeeper adds a number
create -s /shop/job- "b"
ls /shop                           # [config, job-0000000002, job-0000000003, worker-1]

get -w /shop/config                # read and ask to be told about the next change
set /shop/config "retries=5"       # WatchedEvent type:NodeDataChanged path:/shop/config

delete /shop/config
deleteall /shop                    # delete a node and everything under it
quit

blocks.text: The job numbers start at 2 because the counter belongs to the parent and `config` and `worker-1` were created first.

lessons.title: Three ideas that make it useful

rows: Deleted automatically when the client that made it disconnects or stops sending heartbeats
Gets a growing number added to its name
Tells the client once when a node changes; set it again to keep watching

blocks.text: Put the first and third together and you have failure detection. Each worker creates an ephemeral node. Everyone else watches the parent. When a worker dies, its node disappears and the watchers are told.
One ZooKeeper server is a single point of failure, so production runs a group called an ensemble. A change is accepted only when more than half of the servers have it. That majority is the quorum.
Four servers survive no more failures than three, which is why ensembles have an odd size. Three is normal, five for large clusters.
This is a real run of three servers. Each prints its role when asked with `srvr`.

blocks.code:
zk1: Mode: follower     zk2: Mode: follower     zk3: Mode: leader

docker compose stop zk3            # stop the leader
zk1: Mode: follower     zk2: Mode: leader       zk3: down
set /shop v2                       # still works: 2 of 3 is a majority

docker compose stop zk2            # now only 1 of 3
zk1: This ZooKeeper instance is not currently serving requests

docker compose start zk2 zk3
zk1: Mode: follower     zk2: Mode: leader       zk3: Mode: follower
get /shop                          # v2, on the server that was down

blocks.text: One server left alone refuses to answer. That is deliberate. It cannot know whether the other two are dead or merely unreachable, and answering could produce two different truths.

items: One server is the leader. Every write goes through it and is copied to the followers in a fixed order. The protocol is called ZAB.
Reads are answered by whichever server the client is connected to, so a read can be a moment behind.
A client holds a **session** and sends heartbeats. If none arrive within the session timeout, the session expires and its ephemeral nodes are removed.

blocks.text: **Trap.** A long garbage-collection pause looks the same as a crash. The session expires, the node vanishes, and a healthy process loses its role. Timeouts are a trade between fast detection and false alarms.

Every candidate creates an ephemeral sequential node under one parent, for example `/election/n-`. The candidate with the lowest number is the leader. Each other candidate watches only the node just before its own. When the leader dies, its node disappears, exactly one candidate is told, and it takes over.
A lock works the same way: lowest number holds the lock. In Java, use the Curator library for these recipes. The edge cases are hard to get right by hand.
This is from a real two-broker cluster on Kafka 3.6 (image `confluentinc/cp-kafka:7.6.1`) after creating the topic `orders` with 3 partitions and replication factor 2.
Then broker 1, the controller, was stopped:

That is the whole mechanism. Brokers announce themselves with ephemeral nodes. The first broker to create `/controller` becomes the controller. When it dies, the node vanishes, the others are told through a watch, and one of them creates it again.
See the election
A model of three Kafka brokers on ZooKeeper. Stop and start brokers and watch the tree. In the model the lowest running id wins; on a real cluster whichever broker creates the node first wins.

blocks.code:
# zoo.cfg
tickTime=2000                      # heartbeat unit in ms; session timeouts are multiples of it
initLimit=5                        # ticks a follower may take to connect and sync
syncLimit=2                        # ticks a follower may fall behind
dataDir=/data                      # snapshots, and the myid file
dataLogDir=/datalog                # transaction log
server.1=zk1:2888:3888;2181        # 2888 followers to leader, 3888 election, 2181 clients
server.2=zk2:2888:3888;2181
server.3=zk3:2888:3888;2181

blocks.text: Each server also needs a file named `myid` in `dataDir` holding its own number. The Docker image writes both from two environment variables:

blocks.code:
services:
  zk1:
    image: zookeeper:3.9
    hostname: zk1
    environment:
      ZOO_MY_ID: 1
      ZOO_SERVERS: server.1=zk1:2888:3888;2181 server.2=zk2:2888:3888;2181 server.3=zk3:2888:3888;2181
  # zk2 and zk3 are the same with ZOO_MY_ID 2 and 3

blocks.text: ZooKeeper answers short text commands on its client port. Only `srvr` is allowed by default. Allow more with `4lw.commands.whitelist` in the config, or `ZOO_4LW_COMMANDS_WHITELIST=ruok,srvr,mntr` on the Docker image.

blocks.code:
echo ruok | nc localhost 2181      # imok
echo srvr | nc localhost 2181
Zookeeper version: 3.9.7
Latency min/avg/max: 0/0.0/0
Connections: 1
Outstanding: 0
Mode: standalone
Node count: 5
echo mntr | nc localhost 2181      # the same as key and value lines, for a metrics agent
zk_avg_latency  0.0
zk_outstanding_requests  0
zk_znode_count  5

blocks.text: Alert on rising latency, outstanding requests that do not drain, a server that is not a leader or follower, and fewer followers in sync than expected.
Disks and housekeeping

items: Every write is saved to the transaction log before it is confirmed. A slow disk makes the whole ensemble slow, so give the log a fast disk of its own.
Old snapshots and logs are not deleted by default. The Docker image ships with `autopurge.purgeInterval=0`, which means never. Set it to `1` (hours) or the disk fills.
Keep the servers close together. Spreading an ensemble across distant regions adds latency to every write.
Do not store large values, do not use it as a queue, and do not run two servers: two cannot survive one failure.
Two systems to install, secure, monitor and upgrade for one product.
When the controller failed, the new one had to load all metadata from ZooKeeper before it could work. With hundreds of thousands of partitions that took minutes.
Metadata lived in two places, the controller's memory and ZooKeeper, and they could drift apart.

blocks.text: KRaft replaces it. A small group of Kafka nodes called controllers keeps the metadata as a Kafka log and agrees on it with the Raft protocol. Standby controllers already have the data, so failover is quick.

rows: The leader of the controller quorum
Fast, standbys are already in sync
Production-ready from 3.3, the only mode from 4.0

lessons.title: Moving an old cluster to KRaft

blocks.text: You cannot upgrade a ZooKeeper cluster straight to Kafka 4. The path goes through 3.9, the last release that speaks both.

items: Upgrade the cluster to Kafka 3.9.
Start a new KRaft controller quorum with migration enabled. It copies the metadata out of ZooKeeper.
Restart brokers one at a time in migration mode. Metadata is now written to both places, so you can still roll back.
Restart brokers in KRaft mode, then finalize. After that there is no way back.
Shut ZooKeeper down, then upgrade to Kafka 4.

blocks.text: This migration was not run for this guide. Follow the Apache Kafka documentation for your exact version and rehearse it on a copy of the cluster first.
Where ZooKeeper still runs

HBase, Hadoop high availability, SolrCloud and many older Kafka clusters depend on it. The same job is done by etcd in Kubernetes and by ClickHouse Keeper in ClickHouse. The ideas carry over: a small group that agrees by majority, temporary nodes or leases for liveness, and watches for change.
Practice projects

items: Level 1: open two shells. Create an ephemeral node in one, list it from the other, quit the first and list again.
Level 2: run three servers with Compose, stop the leader and find the new one with `srvr`.
Level 3: run Kafka 3.x with ZooKeeper, read `/controller`, stop that broker and read it again.

blocks.title: What is ZooKeeper for?
blocks.text: Holding small shared facts that a cluster must agree on: who is alive, who leads, current configuration. It gives every client the same ordered view of changes.

blocks.title: What is an ephemeral node?
blocks.text: A znode tied to the session that created it. When the session ends or expires, ZooKeeper deletes it. It is how others learn a process has died.

blocks.title: Why an odd number of servers?
blocks.text: Changes need a majority. Four servers tolerate one failure, the same as three, so the extra server adds cost without adding safety.

blocks.title: What happens when the ensemble loses its majority?
blocks.text: The remaining servers stop serving requests. Refusing is safer than letting two halves of a split network accept different writes.

blocks.title: How did Kafka choose its controller with ZooKeeper?
blocks.text: Every broker tried to create the ephemeral node `/controller`. The one that succeeded became controller. The rest watched the node and raced again when it disappeared.

blocks.title: Why did Kafka replace ZooKeeper with KRaft?
blocks.text: To run one system instead of two, to remove the slow metadata reload on controller failover, and to support far more partitions per cluster.

blocks.title: Can a ZooKeeper-based cluster upgrade directly to Kafka 4?
blocks.text: No. Upgrade to 3.9, migrate the metadata to KRaft there, and only then move to 4.

questions.q: Why is Redis fast?
questions.a: Data lives in memory, the structures are simple and purpose-built, and commands run on one thread so there is no locking. Network I/O is multiplexed, so one thread serves thousands of connections.

questions.q: What happens when memory is full?
questions.a: It depends on `maxmemory-policy`. With `noeviction` writes return an error. With an LRU or LFU policy Redis removes keys to make room.

questions.q: MULTI/EXEC or Lua?
questions.a: MULTI runs a fixed list of commands together. Lua can read a value and decide what to write based on it, all in one atomic step. Use Lua when the logic branches.

questions.q: Pub/Sub or Streams?
questions.a: Pub/Sub does not store anything, so offline subscribers miss messages. Streams store entries, support consumer groups and acknowledgements, and can be replayed.

questions.q: How do you keep cache and database consistent?
questions.a: Write the database first, then delete the cache key, and keep a TTL as a safety net. Accept a short stale window, or use change data capture to invalidate when you cannot.

questions.q: Why can Redis lose an acknowledged write?
questions.a: Replication is asynchronous and AOF usually syncs once a second. A crash in that gap loses the latest writes. `WAIT` reduces the risk and does not remove it.

questions.q: What is a hash tag?
questions.a: The part of a key inside braces. In Cluster only that part decides the slot, which lets related keys share a slot so multi-key commands and scripts work.

questions.q: How is Kafka different from a queue like RabbitMQ?
questions.a: A queue hands each message to one worker and deletes it. Kafka keeps an ordered log; each consumer group tracks its own position, so many groups read the same events and can replay them.

questions.q: Where is ordering guaranteed?
questions.a: Within a single partition only. Use the same key for events that must stay in order.

questions.q: Two consumers in one group, one partition. What happens?
questions.a: One consumer gets the partition and the other sits idle as a standby. Parallelism is capped by the partition count.

questions.q: What does acks=all with min.insync.replicas=2 give you?
questions.a: A write succeeds only when at least two replicas have it, so losing one broker loses no acknowledged data. If fewer than two replicas are in sync, the producer gets an error.

questions.q: Why can a consumer see the same event twice?
questions.a: It processed the event and crashed, or lost its partition in a rebalance, before committing the offset. The next owner starts from the last commit.

questions.q: What is consumer lag?
questions.a: The log end offset minus the group's committed offset, per partition. It is the number of events waiting to be processed.

questions.q: When do you use a compacted topic?
questions.a: When consumers need the latest value per key, not the full history: configuration, profiles, a changelog used to rebuild state.

questions.q: What problem does the outbox pattern solve?
questions.a: Writing to a database and publishing to Kafka are two systems, and one can fail after the other succeeded. Writing the event to an outbox table in the same transaction makes them succeed or fail together.

questions.q: Exchange or queue: where does a producer send?
questions.a: Always to an exchange. The exchange uses bindings and the routing key to decide which queues get a copy. Sending "to a queue" uses the default exchange behind the scenes.

questions.q: What is the difference between * and # in a topic binding?
questions.a: `*` matches exactly one word. `#` matches zero or more words. `order.*` matches `order.paid` and not `order.paid.eu`; `order.#` matches both.

questions.q: What happens to a message that matches no queue?
questions.a: It is dropped. To catch these, set an alternate exchange or publish with the mandatory flag so the broker returns it.

questions.q: Why set prefetch?
questions.a: It caps unacknowledged messages per consumer, so work is shared fairly and a slow worker does not hoard messages in memory.

questions.q: What do you need so a broker restart loses nothing?
questions.a: A durable queue, persistent messages, publisher confirms, and manual acknowledgements after the work is done. For a node failure, also a quorum queue.

questions.q: What is a dead letter exchange?
questions.a: An exchange that receives messages a queue gives up on: rejected without requeue, expired, or pushed out by a length limit. It is how failed messages are kept and retried.

questions.q: Classic or quorum queue?
questions.a: Quorum for data that matters, because it is copied to several nodes and survives a node failure. Classic for temporary or rebuildable data on one node.

questions.q: When would you choose Kafka over RabbitMQ?
questions.a: When events must be kept and replayed, when many independent readers need the same stream, or when the volume is very high.

questions.q: Image or container?
questions.a: An image is the read-only package. A container is a running copy of it with its own writable files. Many containers can run from one image.

questions.q: How is a container different from a virtual machine?
questions.a: A virtual machine runs a full operating system. A container is a process on the host's kernel, separated by the operating system, so it is smaller and starts in about a second.

questions.q: What does -p 8080:80 mean?
questions.a: Port 8080 on your machine forwards to port 80 inside the container. Host first, container second.

questions.q: Where does data go when a container is removed?
questions.a: Files in the container are lost. Files in a volume or a bind mount stay.

questions.q: Why can the API reach Redis at the name redis?
questions.a: Compose puts all services on one network, and Docker's built-in name lookup resolves each service name to its container.

questions.q: Why does Kafka in Docker need two listeners?
questions.a: Clients reconnect to the address the broker advertises. Containers need the service name, programs on the host need localhost, so the broker advertises one of each.

questions.q: depends_on is set, yet the app fails at startup. Why?
questions.a: Without a health condition, depends_on waits for the container to start, not for the server to be ready. Add a health check and `condition: service_healthy`, and retry in the app.

questions.q: What is ZooKeeper for?
questions.a: Holding small shared facts that a cluster must agree on: who is alive, who leads, current configuration. It gives every client the same ordered view of changes.

questions.q: What is an ephemeral node?
questions.a: A znode tied to the session that created it. When the session ends or expires, ZooKeeper deletes it. It is how others learn a process has died.

questions.q: Why an odd number of servers?
questions.a: Changes need a majority. Four servers tolerate one failure, the same as three, so the extra server adds cost without adding safety.

questions.q: What happens when the ensemble loses its majority?
questions.a: The remaining servers stop serving requests. Refusing is safer than letting two halves of a split network accept different writes.

questions.q: How did Kafka choose its controller with ZooKeeper?
questions.a: Every broker tried to create the ephemeral node `/controller`. The one that succeeded became controller. The rest watched the node and raced again when it disappeared.

questions.q: Why did Kafka replace ZooKeeper with KRaft?
questions.a: To run one system instead of two, to remove the slow metadata reload on controller failover, and to support far more partitions per cluster.

questions.q: Can a ZooKeeper-based cluster upgrade directly to Kafka 4?
questions.a: No. Upgrade to 3.9, migrate the metadata to KRaft there, and only then move to 4.
